June 10, 2026 
 
The Honorable Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: CMS-0057-P 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
 
Re: 
Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage 
Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children’s Health 
Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of 
Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges (CMS–0062–P) 
 
Dear Administrator Mehmet Oz: 
 
On behalf of the undersigned 17 organizations representing more than 207,000 osteopathic physicians 
(DOs) and medical students, thank you for this opportunity to comment on the 2026 CMS Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule. We appreciate the work that the Centers for 
Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has undertaken to address physician administrative burden and 
the agency’s commitment to pursing reforms that will improve care delivery and access. 
 
Osteopathic physicians are trained in a patient-centered, whole-person approach to care. We believe 
policies should be tailored to empower physicians in partnering with patients to make treatment decisions 
that will result in the best outcomes. The prior authorization (PA) process places substantial time and 
cost burdens on physician practices, and care delays associated with PA often lead to serious adverse 
events among patients. 
 
We commend CMS’ efforts to improve the PA process and extend the requirements from the 2024 
Promoting Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes final rule to cover PA for drugs. 
We commented on the 2024 rulemaking with a request for CMS to address the growing care barriers 
associated with drug PAs and appreciate CMS for its work to be responsive to  our organizations and 
other stakeholder feedback.  
 
This proposed rule makes critical changes that will streamline prior authorization by (1) establishing 
technical standards and requiring use of specific implementation guides that will drive broader electronic 
prior authorization for drugs, (2) ensure that patients and physicians have essential information about 
prior authorizations submitted, (3) improve communication between payors and physicians, and (4) 
create greater accountability in PA processes. Most notably, our organizations urge CMS to finalize 
proposals to require each impacted payor to implement and maintain standards-based application 
programming interfaces (APIs) that support critical functions associated with prior authorization. As 
physicians continue to face interoperability challenges, particularly around the ability to exchange 
information with health plans despite existing API requirements, we support the adoption of standards 
to ensure that data can be shared seamlessly, and PA can be performed for drugs and services within 
physicians’ EMR workflows. 
 
 
Provisions of this rule extend beyond adoption of electronic PA for drugs, and we appreciate CMS’ 
efforts improve the PA process overall. However, we offer the following recommendations to strengthen 
the agency’s proposals and ensure that they fulfill the intended goal of alleviating burden to the greatest 
extent possible: 
 
• Expanding Communication of Prior Authorization Denials for Drugs: While we urge CMS 
to finalize provisions requiring plans to provide physicians and patients with denial reasons for 
denied PA requests, we urge the agency to build upon these provisions by adopting policy that 
will help reduce inappropriate denials. CMS should require potential adverse decisions to be 
reviewed by relevant specialists for the drugs and service prior to issuing any denial and require 
that PA requirements for items and services be based upon publicly available evidence or clinical 
guidelines. CMS already requires that PA denials for items and services in Medicare Advantage 
be reviewed by relevant specialists, and we urge CMS to expand upon this effort.  
 
• Prior Authorization Metrics: While we strongly support CMS’ proposal to require that 
impacted payors annually report PA metrics, we believe that the required metrics are not adequate 
to provide sufficient transparency and build trust with patients. CMS’ proposal would require 
reporting of aggregate data points on approval rates, denial rates, average time elapsed to 
decisions, and other measures regarding prior authorizations at the issuer or contract level. 
However, this reporting will have limited utility to beneficiaries shopping for plans, or providers 
contracting with payers, due to its lack of specificity. Requiring reporting based on specialty, 
therapeutic area, drug, or individual service will provide more meaningful information to patients 
and providers around how plans perform on various prior authorization metrics. Such data would 
also help identify specific services where PA may be inappropriate.  
 
• Timeframes for Prior Authorization Decisions: For most drug prior authorizations across 
impacted payors, CMS proposes that payors make PA determinations no later than 24 hours after 
receiving an urgent request and 72 hours for standard requests. For items and services, CMS’ will 
maintain its requirement of 7 days for standard requests and 72 hours for expedited requests. 
There are also separate timeframes proposed for drugs that are not covered outpatient drugs. In 
general, we appreciate the 24-hour time frame for drugs, but  request the proposed timeframes of 
nondrug requests be shortened to 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for urgent requests. 
Timeframes should be reduced to the greatest extent possible to minimize unnecessary care 
delays. This will ensure patients can receive timely care when they need it. Additionally, we urge 
CMS to consider establishing requirements that plans be capable of issuing real-time decisions 
for PA requests. 
 
While this rule makes important strides in streamlining the prior authorization process and promoting 
transparency for drugs, we urge CMS to continue building on these efforts and pursue comprehensive 
PA reform. Prior authorization burden can be further alleviated by: 
 
1. Limiting the application of PA and step therapy to drugs and services that are truly of concern 
for patient safety, and preventing low-value PA policies that create burden and provide limited 
benefit to patient safety or appropriate utilization; 
 
2. Ensuring that any PA policies are developed by experts in the relevant specialty using publicly 
available evidence-based criteria, and that adverse decisions or peer-reviews are conducted by 
relevant specialists; and 
 
3. Ensuring physicians with strong records of proper documentation and approval for PAs are 
granted relief from requirements through carefully designed gold card programs.   
 
Our organizations greatly appreciate the effort and focus CMS has placed on improving PA and 
addressing burden across its recent rulemaking efforts. We look forward to continuing to work with CMS 
to improve timely access to care, to allow physicians to spend more time with patients, and to adopt PA 
reforms across insurance markets. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
American Osteopathic Association 
American Academy of Osteopathy 
American College of Osteopathic Emergency Physicians 
American College of Osteopathic Internists 
American College of Osteopathic Family Physicians 
American College of Osteopathic Neurologists and Psychiatrists 
American College of Osteopathic Obstetricians and Gynecologists 
American College of Osteopathic Pediatricians

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** American Osteopathic Association and 16 additional osteopathic physician organizations
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Healthcare Provider
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** The undersigned organizations represent more than 207,000 osteopathic physicians (DOs) and medical students. Osteopathic physicians are described as trained in a patient-centered, whole-person approach to care.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The osteopathic physician organizations strongly support CMS's proposal to extend electronic prior authorization requirements to drugs and require standards-based APIs that support PA within physicians' EMR workflows. They ask CMS to strengthen the rule by requiring specialist review and evidence-based criteria for denials, more granular PA metrics by specialty/therapeutic area/drug/service, shorter non-drug PA timeframes, real-time decision capability, limits on low-value PA/step therapy, and gold card relief for high-performing physicians.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** None.
- **Standards referenced:** Standards-based APIs; implementation guides; EMR workflows. No specific IG names are identified in the comment.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Standards-Based APIs for Electronic Prior Authorization**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED / PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Physicians continue to face interoperability challenges exchanging information with health plans, and electronic standards can allow PA to be performed for drugs and services within physicians' EMR workflows.
- **Specific request:** Finalize proposals requiring each impacted payer to implement and maintain standards-based APIs supporting critical PA functions.

**Topic 2: Denial Reasons and Specialist Review**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Denial reasons alone may not reduce inappropriate denials unless adverse decisions are clinically grounded and reviewed by relevant experts.
- **Specific request:** Finalize denial-reason provisions, require potential adverse decisions to be reviewed by relevant specialists before denial, and require PA requirements to be based on publicly available evidence or clinical guidelines.

**Topic 3: Prior Authorization Metrics Granularity**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Aggregate issuer- or contract-level metrics have limited value for beneficiaries shopping for plans and providers contracting with payers.
- **Specific request:** Require PA metrics reporting by specialty, therapeutic area, drug, or individual service to make plan performance transparent and identify areas where PA may be inappropriate.

**Topic 4: Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Shorter timeframes reduce unnecessary care delays and support timely access to needed care.
- **Specific request:** Keep proposed drug timeframes of 72 hours standard and 24 hours urgent where applicable, shorten non-drug item/service timeframes to 72 hours standard and 24 hours urgent, and consider requiring plans to be capable of real-time PA decisions.

**Topic 5: Comprehensive PA and Step Therapy Reform**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Electronic PA reforms alone will not eliminate low-value PA policies or step therapy requirements that create burden with limited patient safety or utilization benefit.
- **Specific request:** Limit PA and step therapy to drugs/services truly of concern for patient safety; require specialty experts to develop evidence-based PA policies; require specialist peer review; and create carefully designed gold card programs for physicians with strong documentation and PA approval records.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1 / S18:** Supports requiring implementation guides and standards-based APIs, emphasizing that required standards are needed for seamless data sharing and PA within EMR workflows.
- **S12 / S21:** Supports extending PA requirements to drugs and views the proposal as responsive to stakeholder concerns about drug PA barriers.
- **S16-S17:** Supports denial-reason requirements and recommends additional protections: specialist review before adverse decisions and publicly available evidence-based criteria.
- **S29-S35:** Supports annual PA metrics but requests more granular reporting by specialty, therapeutic area, drug, or service rather than issuer/contract-level aggregates.
- **S43:** Requests non-drug PA decision timeframes be shortened to 72 hours standard and 24 hours urgent, and asks CMS to consider real-time decision capability.
- **S66-S82:** Responds generally to broader PA/step therapy reform by recommending limits on low-value PA and step therapy, specialty-developed criteria, and gold card programs.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize standards-based API requirements for impacted payers to support critical PA functions.
2. Finalize denial-reason communication provisions for denied drug PA requests.
3. Require potential adverse decisions to be reviewed by relevant specialists before denials are issued.
4. Require PA requirements for items and services to be based on publicly available evidence or clinical guidelines.
5. Require PA metrics reporting by specialty, therapeutic area, drug, or individual service.
6. Shorten non-drug PA timeframes to 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for urgent requests.
7. Consider requiring plans to be capable of issuing real-time PA decisions.
8. Limit PA and step therapy to drugs and services truly of concern for patient safety.
9. Prevent low-value PA policies that create burden with limited patient-safety or appropriate-utilization benefit.
10. Ensure PA policies are developed by relevant specialty experts using publicly available evidence-based criteria.
11. Require adverse decisions or peer reviews to be conducted by relevant specialists.
12. Establish carefully designed gold card programs for physicians with strong documentation and PA approval records.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Physician administrative burden, care delays, serious adverse events, insufficiently granular transparency, inappropriate denials, low-value PA/step therapy, and inadequate non-drug timeframes.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Delayed care, serious adverse events, reduced physician time with patients, diminished trust in plan performance, and unnecessary administrative burden.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Persistent interoperability challenges with health plans despite existing API requirements; lack of specificity in aggregate metrics; payer PA policies not tied to evidence or specialty expertise.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** The organizations represent more than 207,000 osteopathic physicians and medical students.
- **Studies or research referenced:** None cited.
- **Examples provided:** Medicare Advantage already requires relevant specialist review for PA denials for items and services; gold card programs are cited as a model for reducing burden for physicians with strong approval/documentation records.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Osteopathic physicians and medical students, patients, physician practices, impacted payers, health plans, and CMS.
- **Economic implications:** Reducing low-value PA, improving real-time decisioning, and adopting gold card programs could reduce physician practice time and cost burden.
- **Technical feasibility:** The comment supports standards-based APIs and EMR workflow integration but does not provide detailed technical implementation analysis.
- **Patient care impact:** High; the comment links PA delays to serious adverse events and urges faster decisions and clinically appropriate denial review.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with modifications
- **Tone:** Professional, supportive, reform-oriented
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "The prior authorization (PA) process places substantial time and cost burdens on physician practices, and care delays associated with PA often lead to serious adverse events among patients." - Context: Establishes the patient-safety and burden rationale.
2. "Our organizations urge CMS to finalize proposals to require each impacted payor to implement and maintain standards-based application programming interfaces (APIs)." - Context: Core support for standards-based API requirements.
3. "Requiring reporting based on specialty, therapeutic area, drug, or individual service will provide more meaningful information to patients and providers." - Context: Metrics transparency recommendation.
4. "Timeframes should be reduced to the greatest extent possible to minimize unnecessary care delays." - Context: Recommendation for shorter PA decision timeframes.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Requests shorter decision timeframes and real-time PA capabilities.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Highlights time and cost burdens on physician practices.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Central theme; focuses on physician administrative burden and EMR workflow integration.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Supports standards-based APIs to improve data exchange with health plans, though without detailed technical analysis.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Supports requiring specific implementation guides and standards as a driver of broader ePA adoption.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Emphasizes timely care and minimizing unnecessary delays.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Calls for specialty-expert involvement in PA policy development and peer review.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Strong focus on denial reasons and granular PA metrics.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Requests PA be performed within physicians' EMR workflows and supports gold card programs.
